sources.entry: Localization is the process of adapting code and software to other languages.

summary.name: Internationalization and localization
summary.one_liner: Wikipedia article explaining internationalization (i18n) and localization (l10n), the engineering and business processes for adapting software and products to different languages, regions and locales.
use_cases: designing software to support multiple languages
planning a product launch in new countries
handling date, number and currency formats across locales
preparing code for translation with resource files
deciding whether localization is commercially worthwhile
summary.what_it_does: The page defines internationalization as designing software so it can be adapted to languages and regions without engineering changes, and localization as translating text and adding locale-specific components. It covers scope, such as translation, number and date formats, writing direction, pluralization, national conventions, and legal and cultural factors. It describes engineering practice, including splitting locale-dependent code and text into modules, storing strings in resource files and message catalogs, and mentions the gettext library and Unicode CLDR data. It also discusses commercial considerations and examples of localization pitfalls, such as Microsoft Office keyboard shortcuts and translated Excel formula names.
notable: Defines i18n and l10n terminology and explains the numeronym origin
Covers engineering practices such as resource files, message catalogs and gettext
Lists Unicode CLDR as locale data used by Windows, macOS and Debian
Includes historical commercial examples such as Lotus 1-2-3, WordStar and TRS-80 error messages
caveats: This is an encyclopedia article, not a software tool; it describes concepts rather than a product
Some examples are historical and may not reflect current practice
